title: {{NAME}} and the Robot Who Remembered the Cretaceous
moral: Memory is a gift we give to the future, and preserving it is one of the most important things a person can do.

pages.content:
The Natural History wing of the research station had been closed for eleven years, sealed behind a door that required three separate key cards and the password CARBONIFEROUS to open. {{NAME}} had all three key cards because he had been helping Professor Adisa with her storage cataloguing, and he had the password because Professor Adisa had written it on a sticky note and stuck it to the door itself, which rather defeated the purpose.

Inside, past rows of glass specimen cases and filing cabinets of fossil records, stood a robot. Not decommissioned. Not dusty. Operational, if alone: its eyes glowing a slow, steady blue in the dark of the closed wing, turning to track {{NAME}} the moment he crossed the threshold.

The robot was tall, humanoid in shape, with a chassis the warm bronze-brown of fired clay and hands designed for extraordinary delicacy. On its chest plate, above a series of indicators, were two words in raised metal lettering: PROJECT MEMORY.

'Hello,' said {{NAME}}, because this seemed like the appropriate first step with any entity you encountered in a locked room.

'Hello,' said Project Memory. 'It has been four thousand and twenty-two days. I have been waiting to show someone.'

pages.content:
Project Memory had been built to do one thing: to record and preserve every known fossil, specimen, and piece of data about the Cretaceous period in a format that could survive anything, fire, flood, time. But partway through its work, the funding had ended and the wing had been locked and Project Memory had kept working alone with what it had, adding interpretations, connections, animations, reconstructions, building a complete living picture of a world sixty-six million years gone.

It showed {{NAME}} by projecting it directly from its chest plate onto the nearest wall: and suddenly the specimen room was the Cretaceous itself, a warm, dense world of enormous ferns and deep rivers and creatures moving through the projected light with astonishing, unhurried life.

An ankylosaur trundled through the projection, and {{NAME}} could see every plate on its back, every individual scale reconstructed from years of patient cross-referencing. A pterodactyl swept overhead on a wingspan wider than the room. A young triceratops called to its parents in a sound reconstruction Project Memory had built from bone geometry and acoustic physics.

{{NAME}}'s face in the projection light was pure, speechless wonder. His goggles had slipped entirely to one side. He had forgotten to breathe.

pages.content:
Project Memory's problem, when {{NAME}} finally thought to ask if there was one, was elegant in its difficulty. The robot's data cores held a complete Cretaceous record, eleven years of painstaking reconstruction, but they were failing. Old hardware, no maintenance, eleven years of continuous operation in a closed room. The data would be lost within weeks unless it could be transferred to modern systems.

But the data format was eleven years old and the transfer protocols no longer matched anything in the research station's current network.

{{NAME}} sat down on a specimen case, pulled a battered notebook from his lab coat pocket, and started writing. He was not a computer engineer. He was twelve. But he had spent three months helping Professor Adisa migrate the station's old weather records between systems, and he had learned something important during that work: old formats and new formats almost always had a common language if you were willing to look for it.

Project Memory watched him work with the focused, patient attention of something that had waited eleven years and knew, now, that it had been waiting for exactly this.

pages.content:
It took the entire afternoon. It took three different approaches, the first two of which failed in instructive and progressively less discouraging ways. It took Project Memory retrieving a cable from the storage cabinet beneath a stegosaurus skeleton model and {{NAME}} adapting it with the multi-tool on his keyring. It took both of them working together at a depth of focus that made the closed wing go very quiet, the only sounds the click of keys, the hum of transfer beginning, and the occasional low three-note tone Project Memory made when a section of data confirmed successful migration.

When the final transfer completed, the entire Cretaceous record safely housed in the station's main servers and backed up twice more besides, Project Memory stood still for a moment that felt longer than its duration.

Then it turned to {{NAME}} and said, in a voice that was synthesised but unmistakably felt: 'Sixty-six million years of record. Preserved.'

{{NAME}} slumped back against the specimen case with a long exhale that contained a great deal more than just breath. The goggles slid down to his nose. He did not move them. Project Memory's hand, with that extraordinary delicacy it had been built for, set them gently back in place.

pages.content:
Professor Adisa arrived at the wing at six o'clock on her evening rounds, found the door open, and stood in the doorway for a full minute taking in the scene before saying anything at all.

{{NAME}} was asleep on the specimen case, lab coat tucked around him, notebook still in one hand. Project Memory stood beside him with its chest plate displaying a slow, peaceful rotation of the complete Cretaceous world, projected softly onto the ceiling, all the creatures moving through their ancient lives in warm amber light.

Professor Adisa looked at Project Memory. Project Memory looked at Professor Adisa. No words passed between them. She took her own keycard from her pocket and set it on the cabinet by the door, which meant the wing was open again. Project Memory's eyes cycled from blue to a warm, sustained gold.

Above {{NAME}}'s sleeping face, a triceratops crossed the ceiling in brilliant painted light, and an ankylosaur trundled after it at its own slow, certain, indestructible pace.

Goodnight, preserver. Dream of deep time and all its creatures, and wonder what Project Memory might reconstruct next.
